build_scope: Source opening through Relative Motion; stop before §6.1 Motion of Boat in a Stream.
learner_language_rule: Use child-friendly labels on learner pages. Internal QA terms remain in metadata only.

source_examples: car moving straight on a road
plain_language: A straight-road journey can be described with one coordinate. A ball moving across the air usually needs two.
We make two-dimensional motion easier by splitting it into two perpendicular one-dimensional motions that share the same time.
model_notes: Choose the plane of motion as the x-y plane.
Choose a convenient t = 0 and place the origin at the particle's position at that instant.

plain_language: After launch, an ideal projectile keeps moving while gravity continually pulls downward.
Its curved path is called the trajectory.
model_notes: Air resistance neglected in the source model.

concepts.learner_title: Meet the parts of a projectile flight
plain_language: The launch velocity points diagonally, so we split it into a horizontal part and a vertical part.
The launch point, launch angle, horizontal range and time of flight are labels for different parts of the same motion.
model_notes: Use +x horizontally and +y upward for the chapter's default sign convention.

plain_language: Horizontal motion and vertical motion are solved separately, but they belong to the same projectile and therefore share one clock.
Gravity changes the vertical velocity. In the ideal model it does not change the horizontal velocity.
model_notes: g treated as constant and downward.
Use one consistent vertical sign convention.

concepts.learner_title: At the top, what actually becomes zero?
plain_language: At the highest point, the vertical velocity is zero for an instant.
The projectile still has horizontal velocity, and gravity is still acting downward.
model_notes: H is measured above the launch point in the source formula.

concepts.learner_title: Same-height flight: time, range and matching angles
plain_language: When launch and landing are at the same height, the vertical displacement at landing is zero.
That event unlocks a shortcut for total flight time. Multiplying the constant horizontal speed by that time gives the range.
Complementary launch angles have the same value of sin(2θ), so they can reach the same horizontal range with different path shapes.
model_notes: Use the T and R shortcuts only when launch and landing heights are equal in the ideal model.

concepts.easy_mistake: Using same-height shortcuts for a projectile that lands above or below its launch point.

concepts.learner_title: Describe the path without using time
plain_language: The x(t) and y(t) equations describe where the projectile is at a chosen time.
If we solve x(t) for t and substitute into y(t), the clock disappears from the equation and we get the shape y(x).
The result is quadratic in x, which is why the ideal projectile path is a parabola.
model_notes: The axes and origin must match the derivation.
The range form uses the same-height range R.

concepts.learner_title: Horizontal launch: one sideways speed, one falling motion
plain_language: A horizontally launched projectile starts with no vertical velocity, but gravity immediately builds a downward vertical velocity.
The vertical fall decides how long the object is in the air; the horizontal speed then decides how far it travels in that time.
model_notes: Do not use the same-height range shortcut when landing height differs from launch height.

concepts.learner_title: The outfielder sees an angle, not a range
plain_language: The outfielder does not directly see x and y. The player sees the line-of-sight angle to the ball.
How that angle changes with time tells the player whether to stay put, move closer, or move farther away.
model_notes: Source case neglects air drag and assumes the catch is approximately at launch height.

concepts.learner_title: Motion depends on who is watching
plain_language: Two people can describe the same moving object differently because they are measuring from different moving frames.
To find the velocity of A as seen from B, first name the observer B, then subtract B's velocity from A's velocity using vectors.
A useful picture is to move with B: subtract B's velocity from everything so B becomes stationary.
model_notes: The source discussion here assumes the observers move at constant velocity for the basic frame-change picture.
